analysis.one_liner: Extends federal overtime pay protections to truck and bus drivers.
analysis.headline: The bill never left a House subcommittee and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001, without a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal labor law requires most employers to pay time-and-a-half for hours worked beyond 40 a week, but truck and bus drivers have long been carved out of that rule because the Transportation Department sets their maximum hours instead. This one-line bill would delete that carve-out, giving motor carrier employees the same overtime pay rights as most other workers. It was introduced in March 2000, sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, sent again to a subcommittee two months later, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Truck drivers and bus drivers, many of whom work long shifts, would gain the right to overtime pay at time-and-a-half after 40 hours a week, the same protection most other hourly workers already have. The bill's stated subjects also tie the change to safety, since paying for extra hours rather than requiring them for free changes the economics of fatigue.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the exemption in Section 13(b)(1) of the Fair Labor Standards Act, which currently frees motor carrier employers from paying overtime or honoring maximum-hour limits, leaving that to Transportation Department service rules.
After repeal, drivers would be covered by the same overtime guarantee as other covered employees, giving them a legal claim to time-and-a-half pay for long weeks.
The bill's listed subjects include traffic accidents and safety, reflecting the argument that compensating extended hours reduces pressure to drive fatigued.

analysis.who_pays: Trucking and bus companies would bear higher labor costs for employees working over 40 hours a week, and some of that cost could show up in freight rates, bus fares, or tighter scheduling of drivers' hours.

drawbacks.text: Motor carriers would face higher payroll costs, which could be passed through to shipping prices and bus fares or absorbed by restricting drivers' hours.

The Transportation Department already sets maximum hours of service for these drivers, so supporters of the status quo can argue the hours are capped by safety rules and an overtime entitlement is not needed on top of that.
The bill was a single-sentence repeal with no cosponsors and no companion legislation identified in the record, so it never had a working coalition to carry it through the committee process.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to drivers is real and straightforward: the same overtime guarantee most workers already have. The costs fall on a concentrated set of carriers, with some possible pass-through to prices. The bill's weakness is design rather than substance — it is a bare one-line repeal with no transition provisions and no evident effort to build support, which is consistent with it drawing zero cosponsors and going nowhere.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then to its Workforce Protections Subcommittee, which never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Gerald Kleczka introduced the bill on March 22, 2000, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
On May 17, 2000, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, where the record ends.
No hearing, markup, floor action, or vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.
The bill drew no cosponsors at any point.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Motor carriers are better off, since the overtime exemption for their drivers remains intact and their labor costs were never touched. Drivers remain subject to the Department of Transportation's hours rules but without the overtime pay rights most other workers have.

for.name: Rep. Gerald Kleczka
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the motor carrier overtime exemption.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 22, 2000, and sent it to a subcommittee; never reported the bill.

against.name: Subcommittee on Workforce Protections
against.role: Subcommittee of the House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 17, 2000, and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call positions were recorded; a Democrat sponsored it and no members of either party signed on as cosponsors.

industries.note: The bill would have ended the FLSA exemption that lets motor carrier employers avoid paying time-and-a-half after 40 hours, raising payroll costs for long-hour driving schedules. The exemption's survival keeps those costs off the industry's books.
Bus operators are covered by the same motor carrier exemption, so repeal would have made their long-shift drivers eligible for overtime pay, a new cost for the industry.
